blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Fundamental Particles:
Protons, neutrons, and electrons are the fundamental particles of an atom.

Protons and neutrons reside in the nucleus, while electrons orbit the nucleus.

• Particle Charges:

• Protons have a positive charge.

• Neutrons are neutral.

• Electrons have a negative charge, contributing to the atom's charge balance.

• Dalton’s Atomic Theory:
 Matter consists of indivisible atoms, characterized by their weight and type.

• Thomson’s Model:
 Atoms are spheres of positive charge with embedded electrons (plum pudding model).

• Rutherford’s Model:
 Atoms have a dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting around it.

• Bohr’s Model:
 Introduced quantized electron orbits, explaining atomic spectra.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Assumption:

  • Atomic mass is primarily due to the nucleus (protons and neutrons).

blocks.title: Some Important Definitions
blocks.text:
• Isotopes: They are atoms of a given element which have the same atomic number but differ in their mass numbers.
    • Isobars: Isobars are the atoms of different elements which have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
    • Isodiaphers: They are the atoms of different elements which have the same difference of the number of neutrons & protons.
    • Isotones: They are the atoms of different elements which have the same number of neutrons.
    • Isosters: They are the molecules which have the same number of atoms & electrons.
    • Isoelectronic Species: They are the atoms, molecules or ions which have the same number of electrons.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing the charge of electrons and protons:
remember electrons are negative, protons are positive.

• Assuming neutrons contribute to an atom's charge:
they are neutral.

• Misconception:
Confusing Rutherford's model with Bohr’s model.

• Error:
Thinking electrons in Bohr’s model can exist between orbits. Only quantized states are allowed.

Note: Visual aids showing the transition from Thomson's model to Bohr's model can help illustrate atomic structure evolution. Bohr's model's significance in explaining atomic spectra should be emphasized in dedicated study.

modules.name: Electromagnetic Waves (EM Waves) or Radiant Energy

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Electromagnetic Waves

Radio waves, micro waves, Infra-red rays, visible rays, ultraviolet rays, X–rays, gamma rays.

• Wavelength (λ) (Lambda) :
It is defined as the distance between two nearest crests or troughs.

It is measured in terms of Å (Angstrom), pm (picometre), nm (nanometre), cm(centimetre), m (metre)

$1 \, \text{Å} = 10^{-10} \, \text{m}, \quad 1 \, \text{pm} = 10^{-12} \, \text{m}, \quad 1 \, \text{nm} = 10^{-9} \, \text{m}, \quad 1 \, \text{cm} = 10^{-2} \, \text{m}$

• Wave number ($\overline{\nu}$) (nu bar): It is the reciprocal of the wavelength, that is number of waves present in unit length $\overline{\nu} = \frac{1}{\lambda}$

It is measured in terms of  $\text{cm}^{-1} \quad \text{or} \quad \text{m}^{-1}$  etc.

• Frequency ($\nu$) (nu):Frequency of a wave is defined as the number of waves which pass through a point in 1 s. It is measured in terms of hertz (Hz), $\text{s}^{-1}$ or cycle/s(cps) (1 hertz = 1 $\text{s}^{-1}$).

• Time period (T):Time taken by a wave to pass through one point. $T = \frac{1}{\nu}$.

• Velocity (c): Velocity of a wave is defined as distance covered by a wave in 1 second

$c = \frac{\lambda}{T} = \lambda \nu \quad \text{or} \quad \nu = \frac{c}{\lambda} \quad \text{or} \quad c = \nu \, (\text{s}^{-1}) \times \lambda \, (\text{m}) \quad \text{or} \quad c = \nu \lambda \, (\text{m} \, \text{s}^{-1})$

Since c is constant($c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s}$) i.e. frequency ($\nu$) is inversely proportional to wavelength ($\lambda$)

blocks.title: Planck’s Quantum Theory
blocks.text:
• The energy of each quantum
$E = h \nu$ or  $E = \large \frac{hc}{\lambda}$

$h$ is the proportionality constant or

Planck’s constant:

$h = 6.626 \times 10^{-37} \, \text{kJ s} \\ h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \\ h = 6.626 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{erg s}$

• Total amount of energy transmitted from one body to another will be some integral multiple of energy of a quantum.

$E = nh \nu \quad \text{or} \quad E = \large \frac{nhc}{\lambda}
$

where n = Positive integer = Number of quanta or photons

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing frequency and wavelength: General confusion occurs in the relationship between frequency ($\nu$), wavelength (λ), and the speed of light (c).
  • Don't forget the simple equation: $c = \nu \cdot \lambda$  As a result, incorrectly compute one when given the other.
  • Overlooking units: Don't neglect the units (Hz for frequency, meters or centimetres for wavelength, m/s for speed, Joules or electron volts for energy), leading to incorrect results.
  • For instance, forgetting that $1 \, \text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J}$can lead to significant errors in energy calculations.
• Using wrong values of Planck’s constant: Planck's constant has different units depending on the problem, especially in systems where energy is measured in electron volts (eV) or Joules (J). Students must carefully ensure they're using the correct values and units of $h$.

$h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J} \cdot \text{s} \\ h = 6.626 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{erg} \cdot \text{s}$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: The Bohr atomic model was a groundbreaking theory introduced by Niels Bohr. It refined earlier atomic models by incorporating quantum theory to explain the stability of atoms and the emission spectra of hydrogen. Bohr's model made a few key assumptions that advanced our understanding of atomic structure, particularly for hydrogen.

blocks.title: Bohr’s Atomic Model
blocks.text:
• This model was based on quantum theory of radiation and classical laws of physics.

• Bohr model is applicable only for single electron species like $\mathrm{H, He^{+}, Li^{+2}}$ etc.

• The Bohr model is based on the particle nature of electrons.

Electrons can revolve only in those orbits in which angular momentum (mvr) of electron is integral multiple of $\frac{h}{2\pi}$ or

($mvr = n \frac{h}{2\pi} \quad \text{for} \quad n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, \dots$)

blocks.title: Application of Bohr's Model
blocks.text:
• Radius of Various Bohr Orbits (rn)
$\mathrm{r_n=0.529 \times \frac{n^2}{Z} \AA}$

(1 Å = 10-10 m = 10-8 cm, 1nm=10-9 m, 1pm= 10-12 m)

n = 1,2,3,4,5…….

H, He+, Li2+…….

Z = 1,   2,     3,……..

  • Velocity of an electron in Bohr orbit (Vn)
$\mathrm{v_n}=2.188 \times 10^6 \frac{\mathrm{Z}}{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

$\mathrm{v_n}=2.188 \times 10^8 \frac{\mathrm{Z}}{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$

  • Time period of electron in bohr orbit (Tn)
Time taken for complete revolution in nth orbit

= $\frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Velocity}} = \frac{2 \pi r_{n}}{v_{n}} \quad \text{where} \quad T_{n} \propto \frac{n^3}{Z^2}$

  • Frequency of Revolution in bohr orbit ($\nu
$)
Number of revolutions per unit time in nth orbit

= $\frac{\text{Velocity}}{\text{Distance}}$ =$\nu = \frac{v_{n}}{2 \pi r_{n}} \quad \text{where} \quad \nu
 \propto \frac{Z^2}{n^3}$

  • Energy of electron in bohr orbit (En)
$E_n = -\frac{13.6 \, Z^2}{n^2} \, \text{eV/atom}$ (or $E_n = -\frac{2.18 \times 10^{-18} \, Z^2}{n^2} \, \text{J/atom}$)

  • P.E. = (–) 2KE, KE = (–) E, P.E. = 2E
  • Energy difference between two energy levels
$E_{n_2} - E_{n_1} = -13.6 \, Z^2 \left( \frac{1}{n_2^2} - \frac{1}{n_1^2} \right) \, \text{eV}$

  • Important Definitions:
  • Ionization energy:
The minimum amount of energy required to eject an electron from the ground state of an isolated atom is called ionization energy.

n1=1 and n2 = $\infty$

  • Separation energy:
The minimum energy required to escape out electron from its excited state is called separation energy.

n1 = 2,3,4,5…… and n2 = $\infty$

  • Excitation energy:
The amount of energy required to shift an electron from ground state to any excited state is called excitation energy.

n1=1 and n2 = 2,3,4,5…….

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: If the total energy of an electron is –1.51 eV in hydrogen atom then find out K.E, P.E, orbit's radius and velocity of the electron in that orbit.
blocks.answer:
Solution:

(1) $K.E = -E = 1.51 \, \text{eV}$

(2) $P.E = 2 \times E = -2 \times 1.51 = -3.02 \, \text{eV}$

(3) $\because E = -13.6 \times \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \, \text{eV} \\ \text{or} \quad -1.51 = -13.6 \times \frac{2^2}{n^2} \\ \Rightarrow n^2 = \frac{13.6 \times 4}{1.51} = 9 \\ \therefore n = 3 \quad \text{i.e. 3rd orbit}$

(4) $r = 0.529 \times \frac{n^2}{Z} = 0.529 \times \frac{3^2}{1} = 0.529 \times 9 = 4.761 \, \text{Å}$

(5) $v = 2.188 \times 10^8 \times \frac{Z}{n} = 2.188 \times 10^8 \times \frac{1}{3} \, \text{cm/s} = 0.729 \times 10^8 \, \text{cm/s}$
blocks.prompt: If the total energy of an electron is –1.51 eV in hydrogen atom then find out K.E, P.E, orbit's radius and velocity of the electron in that orbit.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: The ionization energy for the hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV then the required energy in eV to excite it from the ground state to 1st excited state.
blocks.answer:
Solution:

Ionization energy = 13.6 eV

i.e. Energy in ground state = –13.6 eV

Energy of Ist excited state

i.e. 2nd orbit = –3.4 eV

so, $E_2 – E_1$ = – 3.4 + 13.6 = 10.2 eV
blocks.prompt: The ionization energy for the hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV then the required energy in eV to excite it from the ground state to 1st excited state.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• The energy levels in the Bohr model are negative, where the energy of an electron becomes less negative as it moves farther from the nucleus. The ground state (closest orbit) has the most negative energy, and higher orbits (excited states) have fewer negative values. Forgetting that the energy levels are negative and interpreting them as positive values.
  • The energy of electrons in atoms is often given in electron volts (eV) or Joules (J). Mixing up units or forgetting to convert between Joules and electron volts, where 1 eV=1.602×10−19 J
  • For calculations involving frequency (ν) and wavelength (λ) of emitted photons, it’s important to use consistent units for Planck’s constant h (usually 6.626×10−34 Js) and the speed of light c (typically 3×108 m/s) in MKS unit system.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Spectrum refers to the range of different energies, frequencies, or wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation emitted or absorbed by atoms or molecules. Spectra provide critical insights into the composition, structure, and behaviour of substances.

blocks.title: Hydrogen Spectrum
blocks.text: The hydrogen spectrum consists of a series of specific wavelengths of light emitted by hydrogen atoms when their electrons transition between energy levels. These transitions lead to distinct spectral lines, which Bohr’s atomic model explains well. The wavelength of various lines show that spectrum lines lie in Visible, Ultraviolet and Infra-red region. These lines are grouped into different series.

blocks.title: Similar Words
blocks.text:
• First line / Starting line / Initial line (λmax. and νmin.)

• Last line / limiting line / marginal line (λmin. and νmax.)

• First line of any series = α line

• Second line of any series = β line
    • Third line of any series = γ line

blocks.title: Rydberg Formula
blocks.text:
$\bar{v}=\frac{1}{\lambda}=\mathrm{RZ}^2\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_1^2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_2^2}\right]$

$\text { where } \mathrm{R}=\text { Rydberg constant }=109678 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}=109700 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}=10970000 \mathrm{~m}^{-1}=1.1 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$

$\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}=9.12 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~cm}=912 \AA$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: In a hydrogen spectrum if electron moves from 7 to 1 orbit by transition in multi steps then find out the total number of lines in the spectrum.
blocks.answer:
Solution:

$\text{Lyman} = (n_2 - 1) = 7 - 1 = 6 \\ \text{Balmer} = (n_2 - 2) = 7 - 2 = 5 \\ \text{Paschen} = (n_2 - 3) = 7 - 3 = 4 \\ \text{Brackett} = (n_2 - 4) = 7 - 4 = 3 \\ \text{Pfund} = (n_2 - 5) = 7 - 5 = 2 \\ \text{Humphrey} = (n_2 - 6) = 7 - 6 = 1 \\ \text{Total} = 21 \\  \text{Total number of lines can be calculated as follows:} \\ \text{Total number of lines} = \frac{(n_2 - n_1) (n_2-n_1 + 1)}{2} = \frac{(7-1) (7 -1+ 1)}{2} = \frac{42}{2} = 21$
blocks.prompt: In a hydrogen spectrum if electron moves from 7 to 1 orbit by transition in multi steps then find out the total number of lines in the spectrum.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: Calculate the wavelength of 1st line of Balmer series in Hydrogen spectrum.
blocks.answer:
Solution:

$\text{For the first line of Balmer series,} \, n_1 = 2, \, n_2 = 3 \\ \frac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2} \right) = R \left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9} \right) \\ = R \left( \frac{9 - 4}{36} \right) = \frac{5R}{36} \\ \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{36}{5R} = \frac{36}{5} \times \frac{1}{R} \\ = \frac{36}{5} \times 9.12 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{cm} = 65.66 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{cm} = 6566 \, \text{Å}$
blocks.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of 1st line of Balmer series in Hydrogen spectrum.

blocks.title: Common Mistake
blocks.text:
• Confusing the series and incorrectly assigning transitions to the wrong series. For example, assuming visible lines (Balmer series) are part of the Lyman series.
  • The Rydberg formula for hydrogen’s spectral lines. Switching $n_2$ and ​ $n_1$ in the formula or substituting them incorrectly​ leads to incorrect wavelength calculations.
  • The wavelength can be calculated in meters or nanometers (nm), depending on the Rydberg constant's units, not converting between meters and nanometers correctly or forgetting that 1 m=109 nm.
  • Confusing absorption and emission, leading to incorrect assumptions about whether energy should be added or released in a transition.

modules.name: Wave Mechanical Model of an Atom

blocks.title: Core concept
blocks.text:
• De-Broglie suggested that if the nature of light is both that of a particle and of a wave, then this dual behavior should be true also for the matter.
    • Heisenberg presented a principle known as Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle which states that: "It is impossible to measure simultaneously the exact position and exact momentum of a body as small as an electron."

blocks.title: Wave Mechanical Model of an Atom
blocks.text:
• The Dual Nature of Matter (The Wave Nature of Electron).
  • Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle.
  • Schrodinger Equation.

blocks.title: The Dual Nature of Matter (The Wave Nature of Electron)
blocks.text:
$\text{According to de Broglie, the wavelength } \lambda \text{ of an electron is inversely proportional to its momentum } p. \\ \lambda = \frac{h}{p} \quad \text{or} \quad \lambda \propto \frac{1}{p} \\ \text{Momentum (} p \text{) = Mass (} m \text{) } \times \text{ Velocity (} v \text{)} \\ \lambda = \frac{h}{mv} \\$

(1) $\text{Bohr's theory and de Broglie concept:} \\ n\lambda = 2\pi r \\$

(2) $\text{de Broglie wave length for kinetic energy of electron:} \\ \lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m \, \text{KE}}} \\$

(3) $\text{de Broglie wave length for electron potential of electron:} \\ \lambda = \sqrt{\frac{150}{V}} \, \text{Å} \quad \text{or} \quad \lambda = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}} \, \text{Å}$

blocks.title: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle
blocks.text: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq \frac{h}{4\pi} \quad \text{or} \quad \Delta x \cdot m \cdot \Delta v \geq \frac{h}{4\pi} \quad \text{or} \quad \Delta E \cdot \Delta t \geq \frac{h}{4\pi}$

blocks.title: Schrodinger Equation
blocks.text:
$H \Psi = E \Psi \\ \text{where } H: \text{ Hamiltonian operator}, \quad \Psi: \text{ wave function}, \quad E: \text{ energy}.$

  • Electrons are described as wave functions, focusing on probability distributions rather than precise locations.
  • Atomic orbital: It is the 3-D space around the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is maximum, approximately 90%.
  • Wave function: The wave function Ψ for an electron in an atom is represented by a set of three quantum numbers, arising naturally as a solution to the Schrödinger equation.
  • Probability density: The probability of finding an electron at a point within an atom is proportional to the square of the orbital wave function $\Psi^2
$ at that point.
$\Psi^2$ is known as probability density and is always positive.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Wrong thinking that the de Broglie wavelength is the same as the wavelength of light.
    • In de Broglie concept, only electrons or tiny particles have wave properties, but the de Broglie wavelength applies to all objects with momentum.
    • The wavelength for macroscopic objects is so small it’s imperceptible. Even baseball has a de Broglie wavelength, but it’s so tiny it can't be observed.
    • In de Broglie mixing up momentum values or using incorrect units, leading to calculation errors
    • Believing the uncertainty principle only refers to limitations in our measuring devices or measurement techniques but the uncertainty principle is a fundamental property of nature, not merely a limitation of measurement tools.
    • Believing the uncertainty principle is only relevant for particles like electrons or photons and does not apply to macroscopic objects but the uncertainty principle is universal and applies to all objects, though its effects are only noticeable for very small particles.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
The mass of a particle is 1 mg and its velocity is $4.5 \times 10^5$ cm per second. What should be the wavelength of this particle if h = $6.625 \times 10^{-27}$erg second.

(1) $1.4722 \times 10^{-24} \, \text{cm}$

(2) $1.4722 \times 10^{-29} \, \text{cm}$

(3) $1.4722 \times 10^{-32} \, \text{cm}$

(4) $1.4722 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{cm}$
blocks.answer:
Solution:

$\text{Given:} \quad m = 1 \, \text{mg} = 1 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{g}, \quad v = 4.5 \times 10^{5} \, \text{cm/s}, \quad h = 6.625 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{erg s}  \text{Then,} $

$\quad \lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$

$= \frac{6.625 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{erg s}}{(1 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{g}) (4.5 \times 10^{5} \, \text{cm/s})}  = 1.4722 \times 10^{-29} \, \text{cm}$
blocks.prompt: The mass of a particle is 1 mg and its velocity is $4.5 \times 10^5$ cm per second. What should be the wavelength of this particle if h = $6.625 \times 10^{-27}$erg second.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Quantum numbers are essential to understanding the structure of atoms and describe the properties of electrons within atoms. They arise from the quantum mechanical solutions to the Schrödinger equation for the electron in an atom, where each quantum number represents a different aspect of an electron’s behavior or position. There are four quantum numbers.

blocks.title: 1. Principal Quantum Number (n)
blocks.text:
• It represents the name and energy of the shell to which electron belongs and size of orbit.
  • The value of n lies between 1 to ∞
  • n = 1,2,3,4– – – – – corresponding name of shells are K, L, M, N, O, – – – – –
  • The number of electrons in a particular shell = 2n2
  • The total number of orbitals in a particular shell = n2

blocks.title: 2. Azimuthal quantum number (l)
blocks.text:
• It represents the name of the subshell, shape of orbital and orbital angular momentum
  • Possible values of $l$ are: -
  • $l$ = 0, 1, 2 ---------------- (n –1)
  • $l$ = 0 → s Subshell (Spherical shape)
  • $l$ = 1 → p Subshell (Dumb Bell shape)
  • $l$ = 2 → d Subshell (Double Dumb Bell shape)
  • $l$ = 3 → f Subshell (Complex shape)
  • The number of electrons in a particular sub shell = 2(2$l$+1)
  • The orbital angular momentum = $\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)} \frac{\mathrm{h}}{2 \pi}$

blocks.title: 3. Magnetic Quantum Number (m)
blocks.text:
• Value of m = all integral value from – $l$ to +$l$ including zero.

(– $l$…-3, -2, -1, 0, +1, +2, +3… +$l$)

  • Total values of m (or total number of orbitals) =2$l$+1

blocks.title: 4. Spin Quantum number (s)
blocks.text:
• It represents the direction of electron spin around its own axis.

• For clockwise spin/spin up ($\uparrow$) electron  $+ \frac{1}{2} $ (or  $- \frac{1}{2} $)

• For anticlockwise spin/spin down ($\downarrow$) electron  $- \frac{1}{2} $  (or  $+ \frac{1}{2}  $)

  • Spin angular momentum of an electron =  $\frac{h}{2\pi} \sqrt{s(s+1)}$

blocks.title: Node
blocks.text:
It is point /line/plane/surface in which probability of finding electron is zero.

Number of Radial nodes / Spherical nodes / Nodal surface in an orbital in a subshell = $n-l-1$

Number of Angular nodes / Nodal planes in an orbital in a sub shell= $l$

Total Node= $n$ $-1$

blocks.title: Nodal plane
blocks.text:
s orbitals = no nodal plane

p orbitals =   px → yz nodal plane

py → xz nodal plane

pz → xy nodal plane

d orbitals =  $d_{xy}$ → xz & yz nodal plane

$d_{xz}$ → xy & zy nodal plane

$d_{yz}$ → zx & yx nodal plane

$d_{x^2-y^2}$ → 2 nodal planes

$d_{z^2}$ → 0 nodal planes

f orbitals = complex

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Misunderstanding the specific role of each quantum number, for instance, wrong thinking that the principal quantum number n determines the shape of an orbital.
  • The value of $l$ is always less than the n $(l < n)$ so that 1p, 2d, 3f sub shells are not possible.
  • The value of m is always less than or equal to the $l (m ≤ l)$.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Electrons are added to atomic orbitals in a specific order to achieve the most stable (lowest energy) electron configuration. Following these principles ensures accurate prediction of the electronic configuration of atoms and their chemical properties.

blocks.title: Aufbau Principle
blocks.text:
• The Aufbau principle gives a sequence in which various subshells are filled up depending on the relative order of the energies of various subshells.
  • The subshell with minimum energy is filled up first when this subshell obtained maximum quota of electrons then the next subshell of higher energy starts filling.

blocks.title: (n + l) Rule (For multi electron species)
blocks.text:
The subshell with lowest (n + l) value is filled up first. When two or more subshell have same (n+l) value then the subshell with lowest value of n is filled up first.

Order for filling subshells: 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, 3s2, 3p6, 4s2, 3d10, 4p6, 5s2, 4d10, 5p6, 6s2, 4f14, 5d10, 6p6, 7s2, 5f14, 6d10……....

blocks.title: Hund's Maximum Multiplicity Rule
blocks.text: Electrons will fill degenerate orbitals singly before pairing up. In other words, for orbitals of the same energy (like the three p-orbitals in a p-subshell), one electron is placed in each orbital with parallel spins before any orbital gets a second electron.

blocks.title: Pauli's Exclusion Principle
blocks.text:
• Pauli stated that no two electrons in an atom can have the same values as all four quantum numbers.
  • An orbital can accommodate a maximum of 2 electrons with opposite spin.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
The maximum number of such electrons in an atom with quantum number n = 3, l = 2 is:

(1) 2

(2) 6

(3) 10

(4) 14
blocks.answer: It is a 3d subshell and the total number of electrons are 10.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
In potassium the probable order of energy level for 19th electron is:

(1) 3s > 3d

(2) 4s < 3d

(3) 4s > 4p

(4) 4s = 3d
blocks.answer: According to (n+l) rule 4s has lower energy as compared to the 3d.

blocks.title: Some Special Points
blocks.text:
• Total spin =  $\pm \frac{1}{2}$ x  no. of unpaired electron.
    • Magnetic moment ($\mu$) =$\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ B.M. Where ‘n’ is no. of unpaired electron
    • Paramagnetic: Those species which contain one or more than one unpaired electron.
    • Diamagnetic: Those species which do not contain any unpaired electrons.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Always fill the lowest energy orbitals first. Use the order of filling based on the periodic table or the (n+l) rule to ensure proper sequence.
  • In hund rule, fill each degenerate orbital singly first, with parallel spins, before pairing electrons in any of those orbitals. This minimizes electron-electron repulsion
  • In Pauli Exclusion Principle, ensure that each electron in the same orbital has opposite spins.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Fundamental Particles:
Protons, neutrons, and electrons are the fundamental particles of an atom.

Protons and neutrons reside in the nucleus, while electrons orbit the nucleus.

• Particle Charges:

• Protons have a positive charge.

• Neutrons are neutral.

• Electrons have a negative charge, contributing to the atom's charge balance.

• Dalton’s Atomic Theory:
 Matter consists of indivisible atoms, characterized by their weight and type.

• Thomson’s Model:
 Atoms are spheres of positive charge with embedded electrons (plum pudding model).

• Rutherford’s Model:
 Atoms have a dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting around it.

• Bohr’s Model:
 Introduced quantized electron orbits, explaining atomic spectra.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Assumption:

  • Atomic mass is primarily due to the nucleus (protons and neutrons).

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Electromagnetic Waves

Radio waves, micro waves, Infra-red rays, visible rays, ultraviolet rays, X–rays, gamma rays.

• Wavelength (λ) (Lambda) :
It is defined as the distance between two nearest crests or troughs.

It is measured in terms of Å (Angstrom), pm (picometre), nm (nanometre), cm(centimetre), m (metre)

$1 \, \text{Å} = 10^{-10} \, \text{m}, \quad 1 \, \text{pm} = 10^{-12} \, \text{m}, \quad 1 \, \text{nm} = 10^{-9} \, \text{m}, \quad 1 \, \text{cm} = 10^{-2} \, \text{m}$

• Wave number ($\overline{\nu}$) (nu bar): It is the reciprocal of the wavelength, that is number of waves present in unit length $\overline{\nu} = \frac{1}{\lambda}$

It is measured in terms of  $\text{cm}^{-1} \quad \text{or} \quad \text{m}^{-1}$  etc.

• Frequency ($\nu$) (nu):Frequency of a wave is defined as the number of waves which pass through a point in 1 s. It is measured in terms of hertz (Hz), $\text{s}^{-1}$ or cycle/s(cps) (1 hertz = 1 $\text{s}^{-1}$).

• Time period (T):Time taken by a wave to pass through one point. $T = \frac{1}{\nu}$.

• Velocity (c): Velocity of a wave is defined as distance covered by a wave in 1 second

$c = \frac{\lambda}{T} = \lambda \nu \quad \text{or} \quad \nu = \frac{c}{\lambda} \quad \text{or} \quad c = \nu \, (\text{s}^{-1}) \times \lambda \, (\text{m}) \quad \text{or} \quad c = \nu \lambda \, (\text{m} \, \text{s}^{-1})$

Since c is constant($c = 3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s}$) i.e. frequency ($\nu$) is inversely proportional to wavelength ($\lambda$)

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: The Bohr atomic model was a groundbreaking theory introduced by Niels Bohr. It refined earlier atomic models by incorporating quantum theory to explain the stability of atoms and the emission spectra of hydrogen. Bohr's model made a few key assumptions that advanced our understanding of atomic structure, particularly for hydrogen.

blocks.title: Bohr’s Atomic Model
blocks.text:
• This model was based on quantum theory of radiation and classical laws of physics.

• Bohr model is applicable only for single electron species like $\mathrm{H, He^{+}, Li^{+2}}$ etc.

• The Bohr model is based on the particle nature of electrons.

Electrons can revolve only in those orbits in which angular momentum (mvr) of electron is integral multiple of $\frac{h}{2\pi}$ or

($mvr = n \frac{h}{2\pi} \quad \text{for} \quad n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, \dots$)

blocks.title: Hydrogen Spectrum
blocks.text: The hydrogen spectrum consists of a series of specific wavelengths of light emitted by hydrogen atoms when their electrons transition between energy levels. These transitions lead to distinct spectral lines, which Bohr’s atomic model explains well. The wavelength of various lines show that spectrum lines lie in Visible, Ultraviolet and Infra-red region. These lines are grouped into different series.

blocks.title: Similar Words
blocks.text:
• First line / Starting line / Initial line (λmax. and νmin.)

• Last line / limiting line / marginal line (λmin. and νmax.)

• First line of any series = α line

• Second line of any series = β line
    • Third line of any series = γ line

blocks.title: 1. Principal Quantum Number (n)
blocks.text:
• It represents the name and energy of the shell to which electron belongs and size of orbit.
  • The value of n lies between 1 to ∞
  • n = 1,2,3,4– – – – – corresponding name of shells are K, L, M, N, O, – – – – –
  • The number of electrons in a particular shell = 2n2
  • The total number of orbitals in a particular shell = n2

blocks.title: 2. Azimuthal quantum number (l)
blocks.text:
• It represents the name of the subshell, shape of orbital and orbital angular momentum
  • Possible values of $l$ are: -
  • $l$ = 0, 1, 2 ---------------- (n –1)
  • $l$ = 0 → s Subshell (Spherical shape)
  • $l$ = 1 → p Subshell (Dumb Bell shape)
  • $l$ = 2 → d Subshell (Double Dumb Bell shape)
  • $l$ = 3 → f Subshell (Complex shape)
  • The number of electrons in a particular sub shell = 2(2$l$+1)
  • The orbital angular momentum = $\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)} \frac{\mathrm{h}}{2 \pi}$

blocks.title: 3. Magnetic Quantum Number (m)
blocks.text:
• Value of m = all integral value from – $l$ to +$l$ including zero.

(– $l$…-3, -2, -1, 0, +1, +2, +3… +$l$)

  • Total values of m (or total number of orbitals) =2$l$+1

blocks.title: 4. Spin Quantum number (s)
blocks.text:
• It represents the direction of electron spin around its own axis.

• For clockwise spin/spin up ($\uparrow$) electron  $+ \frac{1}{2} $ (or  $- \frac{1}{2} $)

• For anticlockwise spin/spin down ($\downarrow$) electron  $- \frac{1}{2} $  (or  $+ \frac{1}{2}  $)

  • Spin angular momentum of an electron =  $\frac{h}{2\pi} \sqrt{s(s+1)}$

blocks.title: Node
blocks.text:
It is point /line/plane/surface in which probability of finding electron is zero.

Number of Radial nodes / Spherical nodes / Nodal surface in an orbital in a subshell = $n-l-1$

Number of Angular nodes / Nodal planes in an orbital in a sub shell= $l$

Total Node= $n$ $-1$

blocks.title: Nodal plane
blocks.text:
s orbitals = no nodal plane

p orbitals =   px → yz nodal plane

py → xz nodal plane

pz → xy nodal plane

d orbitals =  $d_{xy}$ → xz & yz nodal plane

$d_{xz}$ → xy & zy nodal plane

$d_{yz}$ → zx & yx nodal plane

$d_{x^2-y^2}$ → 2 nodal planes

$d_{z^2}$ → 0 nodal planes

f orbitals = complex

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Electrons are added to atomic orbitals in a specific order to achieve the most stable (lowest energy) electron configuration. Following these principles ensures accurate prediction of the electronic configuration of atoms and their chemical properties.

blocks.title: Aufbau Principle
blocks.text:
• The Aufbau principle gives a sequence in which various subshells are filled up depending on the relative order of the energies of various subshells.
  • The subshell with minimum energy is filled up first when this subshell obtained maximum quota of electrons then the next subshell of higher energy starts filling.

blocks.title: (n + l) Rule (For multi electron species)
blocks.text:
The subshell with lowest (n + l) value is filled up first. When two or more subshell have same (n+l) value then the subshell with lowest value of n is filled up first.

Order for filling subshells: 1s2, 2s2, 2p6, 3s2, 3p6, 4s2, 3d10, 4p6, 5s2, 4d10, 5p6, 6s2, 4f14, 5d10, 6p6, 7s2, 5f14, 6d10……....

blocks.title: Pauli's Exclusion Principle
blocks.text:
• Pauli stated that no two electrons in an atom can have the same values as all four quantum numbers.
  • An orbital can accommodate a maximum of 2 electrons with opposite spin.

    • Paramagnetic: Those species which contain one or more than one unpaired electron.
    • Diamagnetic: Those species which do not contain any unpaired electrons.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing the charge of electrons and protons:
remember electrons are negative, protons are positive.

• Assuming neutrons contribute to an atom's charge:
they are neutral.

• Misconception:
Confusing Rutherford's model with Bohr’s model.

• Error:
Thinking electrons in Bohr’s model can exist between orbits. Only quantized states are allowed.

Note: Visual aids showing the transition from Thomson's model to Bohr's model can help illustrate atomic structure evolution. Bohr's model's significance in explaining atomic spectra should be emphasized in dedicated study.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing frequency and wavelength: General confusion occurs in the relationship between frequency ($\nu$), wavelength (λ), and the speed of light (c).
  • Don't forget the simple equation: $c = \nu \cdot \lambda$  As a result, incorrectly compute one when given the other.
  • Overlooking units: Don't neglect the units (Hz for frequency, meters or centimetres for wavelength, m/s for speed, Joules or electron volts for energy), leading to incorrect results.
  • For instance, forgetting that $1 \, \text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{J}$can lead to significant errors in energy calculations.
• Using wrong values of Planck’s constant: Planck's constant has different units depending on the problem, especially in systems where energy is measured in electron volts (eV) or Joules (J). Students must carefully ensure they're using the correct values and units of $h$.

$h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J} \cdot \text{s} \\ h = 6.626 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{erg} \cdot \text{s}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• The energy levels in the Bohr model are negative, where the energy of an electron becomes less negative as it moves farther from the nucleus. The ground state (closest orbit) has the most negative energy, and higher orbits (excited states) have fewer negative values. Forgetting that the energy levels are negative and interpreting them as positive values.
  • The energy of electrons in atoms is often given in electron volts (eV) or Joules (J). Mixing up units or forgetting to convert between Joules and electron volts, where 1 eV=1.602×10−19 J
  • For calculations involving frequency (ν) and wavelength (λ) of emitted photons, it’s important to use consistent units for Planck’s constant h (usually 6.626×10−34 Js) and the speed of light c (typically 3×108 m/s) in MKS unit system.

blocks.title: Common Mistake
blocks.text:
• Confusing the series and incorrectly assigning transitions to the wrong series. For example, assuming visible lines (Balmer series) are part of the Lyman series.
  • The Rydberg formula for hydrogen’s spectral lines. Switching $n_2$ and ​ $n_1$ in the formula or substituting them incorrectly​ leads to incorrect wavelength calculations.
  • The wavelength can be calculated in meters or nanometers (nm), depending on the Rydberg constant's units, not converting between meters and nanometers correctly or forgetting that 1 m=109 nm.
  • Confusing absorption and emission, leading to incorrect assumptions about whether energy should be added or released in a transition.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Wrong thinking that the de Broglie wavelength is the same as the wavelength of light.
    • In de Broglie concept, only electrons or tiny particles have wave properties, but the de Broglie wavelength applies to all objects with momentum.
    • The wavelength for macroscopic objects is so small it’s imperceptible. Even baseball has a de Broglie wavelength, but it’s so tiny it can't be observed.
    • In de Broglie mixing up momentum values or using incorrect units, leading to calculation errors
    • Believing the uncertainty principle only refers to limitations in our measuring devices or measurement techniques but the uncertainty principle is a fundamental property of nature, not merely a limitation of measurement tools.
    • Believing the uncertainty principle is only relevant for particles like electrons or photons and does not apply to macroscopic objects but the uncertainty principle is universal and applies to all objects, though its effects are only noticeable for very small particles.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Misunderstanding the specific role of each quantum number, for instance, wrong thinking that the principal quantum number n determines the shape of an orbital.
  • The value of $l$ is always less than the n $(l < n)$ so that 1p, 2d, 3f sub shells are not possible.
  • The value of m is always less than or equal to the $l (m ≤ l)$.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Always fill the lowest energy orbitals first. Use the order of filling based on the periodic table or the (n+l) rule to ensure proper sequence.
  • In hund rule, fill each degenerate orbital singly first, with parallel spins, before pairing electrons in any of those orbitals. This minimizes electron-electron repulsion
  • In Pauli Exclusion Principle, ensure that each electron in the same orbital has opposite spins.

blocks.title: Planck’s Quantum Theory
blocks.text:
• The energy of each quantum
$E = h \nu$ or  $E = \large \frac{hc}{\lambda}$

$h$ is the proportionality constant or

Planck’s constant:

$h = 6.626 \times 10^{-37} \, \text{kJ s} \\ h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \, \text{J s} \\ h = 6.626 \times 10^{-27} \, \text{erg s}$

• Total amount of energy transmitted from one body to another will be some integral multiple of energy of a quantum.

$E = nh \nu \quad \text{or} \quad E = \large \frac{nhc}{\lambda}
$

where n = Positive integer = Number of quanta or photons

blocks.title: Application of Bohr's Model
blocks.text:
• Radius of Various Bohr Orbits (rn)
$\mathrm{r_n=0.529 \times \frac{n^2}{Z} \AA}$

(1 Å = 10-10 m = 10-8 cm, 1nm=10-9 m, 1pm= 10-12 m)

n = 1,2,3,4,5…….

H, He+, Li2+…….

Z = 1,   2,     3,……..

  • Velocity of an electron in Bohr orbit (Vn)
$\mathrm{v_n}=2.188 \times 10^6 \frac{\mathrm{Z}}{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

$\mathrm{v_n}=2.188 \times 10^8 \frac{\mathrm{Z}}{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$

  • Time period of electron in bohr orbit (Tn)
Time taken for complete revolution in nth orbit

= $\frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Velocity}} = \frac{2 \pi r_{n}}{v_{n}} \quad \text{where} \quad T_{n} \propto \frac{n^3}{Z^2}$

  • Frequency of Revolution in bohr orbit ($\nu
$)
Number of revolutions per unit time in nth orbit

= $\frac{\text{Velocity}}{\text{Distance}}$ =$\nu = \frac{v_{n}}{2 \pi r_{n}} \quad \text{where} \quad \nu
 \propto \frac{Z^2}{n^3}$

  • Energy of electron in bohr orbit (En)
$E_n = -\frac{13.6 \, Z^2}{n^2} \, \text{eV/atom}$ (or $E_n = -\frac{2.18 \times 10^{-18} \, Z^2}{n^2} \, \text{J/atom}$)

  • P.E. = (–) 2KE, KE = (–) E, P.E. = 2E
  • Energy difference between two energy levels
$E_{n_2} - E_{n_1} = -13.6 \, Z^2 \left( \frac{1}{n_2^2} - \frac{1}{n_1^2} \right) \, \text{eV}$

  • Important Definitions:
  • Ionization energy:
The minimum amount of energy required to eject an electron from the ground state of an isolated atom is called ionization energy.

n1=1 and n2 = $\infty$

  • Separation energy:
The minimum energy required to escape out electron from its excited state is called separation energy.

n1 = 2,3,4,5…… and n2 = $\infty$

  • Excitation energy:
The amount of energy required to shift an electron from ground state to any excited state is called excitation energy.

n1=1 and n2 = 2,3,4,5…….

blocks.title: Rydberg Formula
blocks.text:
$\bar{v}=\frac{1}{\lambda}=\mathrm{RZ}^2\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_1^2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_2^2}\right]$

$\text { where } \mathrm{R}=\text { Rydberg constant }=109678 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}=109700 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}=10970000 \mathrm{~m}^{-1}=1.1 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$

$\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}=9.12 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~cm}=912 \AA$

blocks.text:
$\text{According to de Broglie, the wavelength } \lambda \text{ of an electron is inversely proportional to its momentum } p. \\ \lambda = \frac{h}{p} \quad \text{or} \quad \lambda \propto \frac{1}{p} \\ \text{Momentum (} p \text{) = Mass (} m \text{) } \times \text{ Velocity (} v \text{)} \\ \lambda = \frac{h}{mv} \\$

(1) $\text{Bohr's theory and de Broglie concept:} \\ n\lambda = 2\pi r \\$

(2) $\text{de Broglie wave length for kinetic energy of electron:} \\ \lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m \, \text{KE}}} \\$

blocks.title: Schrodinger Equation
blocks.text:
$H \Psi = E \Psi \\ \text{where } H: \text{ Hamiltonian operator}, \quad \Psi: \text{ wave function}, \quad E: \text{ energy}.$

  • Electrons are described as wave functions, focusing on probability distributions rather than precise locations.
  • Atomic orbital: It is the 3-D space around the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is maximum, approximately 90%.
  • Wave function: The wave function Ψ for an electron in an atom is represented by a set of three quantum numbers, arising naturally as a solution to the Schrödinger equation.
  • Probability density: The probability of finding an electron at a point within an atom is proportional to the square of the orbital wave function $\Psi^2
$ at that point.
$\Psi^2$ is known as probability density and is always positive.
